article.overview: A charged particle detector is a scientific instrument that measures electrically charged particles, such as electrons, protons and heavier ions, and records how many arrive and how much energy each carries. Charged particles reach the Moon from the Sun, from galactic cosmic rays and from the plasma of the Earth's magnetic tail, and a detector on the surface or in orbit records what arrives there [1][4].
article.description:
A charged particle detector is a family of instrument designs rather than a single standard device. Most have an entrance aperture that admits particles, a sensing element that produces an electrical pulse when a particle is detected, and electronics that count pulses and sort them by energy, direction or particle type. The Apollo 14 CPLEE used electrostatic deflection with electron multipliers to sort particles by energy [1]. The Chang'e-4 LND used a stack of silicon detectors that stop particles and record the energy they deposit [4].

Surface instruments measure the particle environment at the place where they sit, while orbital instruments measure it along the spacecraft's path. The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER) is an orbital example. The LND paper reports that CRaTER measured a radiation exposure of about 0.22 to 0.27 mGy per day in its 50 km orbit, citing a CRaTER measurement reference [4]. Its instrument paper is Spence et al. (2010) [5]. The same paper reports that the Chandrayaan-1 Radiation Dose Monitor (RADOM) measured 0.227 mGy per day averaged over 20 November 2008 to 18 May 2009 in its 100 km orbit, rising to 0.257 mGy per day in a later 200 km phase [4]. A secondary summary describes CRaTER as measuring energy transfer by charged particles in lunar orbit [6]. Its detailed specifications are not verified in this article.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
Charged particle detectors at the Moon serve three main purposes. The first is to characterise the local plasma and particle environment. The Apollo 14 CPLEE was designed to measure the energy spectra of low-energy electrons and ions striking the lunar surface. Its primary purpose was to examine plasma particles from the Sun and low-energy particle flux in the Earth's magnetic tail [1][2].

The second purpose is radiation dose measurement. The chief scientific goal of the Chang'e-4 LND is to obtain the first active dosimetric measurements on the lunar surface, and the paper states that its dose data are intended to support future human lunar missions [4].

The third purpose is solar and heliospheric science. The LND paper describes coarse charged particle spectra, composition measurement and energy spectra up to 30 MeV per nucleon, which it links to the knee in the interplanetary energy spectrum and to particle acceleration. It also lists the onset times of solar particle events as a science objective [4].
article.operating_principle:
Two sensing principles appear in the examples in this article. The CPLEE used an electrostatic analyser. Incoming particles pass through a series of slits and between two deflection plates. A voltage on the plates selects which particle energies reach the detectors, and the voltage is stepped through a fixed sequence of levels [1]. Five small-aperture channel electron multipliers measure one particle polarity at each step, while a larger multiplier measures the opposite polarity [1]. A channel electron multiplier is a hollow glass tube that emits secondary electrons when struck by a particle. The cascade multiplies a single arrival to a pulse with a gain of the order of 10^7 by the time it reaches the anode [1].

The LND used a solid-state telescope. Ten segmented silicon detectors, each 500 micrometres thick, form a stack. A particle that enters the front detector deposits part of its energy there, and the rest is deposited in the detectors behind it. Combining these two measurements allows the instrument to estimate the particle's energy and, for particles that stop within the stack, its composition [4]. The same stack also records neutral particles, such as fast and thermal neutrons and gamma rays, which the LND separates from charged-particle events [4].
article.scientific_importance:
Direct measurements of the radiation environment near the Moon are scarce. The LND paper states that radiation measurements in the vicinity of the Moon are remarkably scarce, and that Chandrayaan-1 and LRO were the only recent missions to report such data apart from Apollo 17 subsurface neutron measurements [4]. Surface measurements therefore complement orbital data rather than duplicating it.

The Apollo 14 CPLEE gave a surface view of low-energy plasma. Its 1971 preliminary report summarises a stable, low-energy photoelectron flux at the lunar surface, which the report attributes to solar photons striking the surface material, and plasma clouds produced by the impact of the Apollo 14 lunar module ascent stage [2]. The Chang'e-4 LND adds a second surface dataset from the lunar far side, in a different epoch and with a different detector design [4].

Measurements of this kind also constrain dose estimates for crew. The LND paper notes that the dose data must be interpreted with the lander's own background in mind before they can be used to predict human exposure on the surface [4].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a charged particle detector. Flown examples range from a sealed analyser box on legs, a few kilograms in mass, to a segmented solid-state telescope mounted inside a lander compartment. The values below describe two flown instruments only and must not be generalised. Both examples are documented from flight-era or post-flight sources [1][2][4].

examples.name: Apollo 14 Charged Particle Lunar Environment Experiment (CPLEE)
examples.type: Flown lunar surface instrument (Apollo 14 ALSEP, operated 1971 to 1977)
examples.energy_range_preliminary_report_1971: 50 eV to 50 000 eV (as stated in the 1971 preliminary report summary)
examples.sensor_configuration: Box on four legs containing two charged-particle analysers (A and B), two programmable high-voltage supplies and twelve 20-bit accumulators. Each analyser has five C-shaped channel electron multipliers (nominal 1 mm aperture) and one helical channel electron multiplier (nominal 8 mm aperture).
examples.look_directions: Analyser A: local lunar vertical. Analyser B: 60 degrees from vertical toward lunar west.
examples.timing: Deflection-plate voltage stepped through a fixed sequence; 1.2 s accumulation per sensor; 2.4 s per voltage step; 19.2 s cycle.
examples.deployment: Deployed on the lunar surface on 5 February 1971, about 3 m northeast of the ALSEP central station; levelled to 1.7 degrees and aligned east-west with a sun compass; dust cover removed after lunar module ascent.
examples.calibration: Nickel-63 radioactive source under the dust cover allowed on-Moon proof calibration.
examples.operational_history: Analyser B power supply failed 8 April 1971; analyser A partial power-supply failure 6 June 1971; intermittent operation from 1971; voltage problems from high temperatures in 1972; signal losses and reacquisitions from 1975 to 1977; standby when ALSEP stations were shut off on 30 September 1977.

examples.name: Chang'e-4 Lunar Lander Neutron and Dosimetry (LND) experiment
examples.type: Flown lunar surface instrument (Chang'e-4 lander payload, 2019 onward)
examples.mass_note: Instrument mass not stated in the paper text retrieved for this article. The paper's dose calculation uses the mass of one silicon detector, 1.04 g; this is a component value and not the instrument mass [4].
examples.power_note: Not stated in the paper text retrieved for this article; the sensor head and electronics box receive power and heater supply from the lander through harnesses.
examples.detector_configuration: Sensor head with ten segmented 500 micrometre thick silicon solid-state detectors (A to J) arranged as a telescope; separate electronics box connected to the lander Instrument Control Unit. Thermal neutron detection uses a 20 micrometre gadolinium foil between detector pairs E and F and between G and H, with 250 micrometre gadolinium foils shielding those pairs from thermal neutrons coming from below [4].
examples.energy_range: Energy spectra up to 30 MeV per nucleon (charged particles).
measurement_outputs: Time series of charged and neutral particle dose rate in silicon (cadence up to 1 minute)
Coarse LET spectra (cadence up to 1 minute)
Coarse charged particle spectra (cadence up to 1 minute)
Coarse energy deposit spectrum of neutral particles (cadence up to 1 minute)
examples.mounting: Sensor head on a bracket near the lander upper deck, inside the -Y payload compartment; tilted 13 degrees from the normal to the lander deck; re-closeable top window gives a field of view to the sky.
examples.window_operation: Open during the lunar day, closed during the cold lunar night.
examples.first_lunar_day_temperature_note: Highest temperatures on the sensor head analogue board, lowest in the electronics box.
examples.background_note: Lander RTG and three RHUs produce background that dominates small energy deposits in single detectors and must be accounted for.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The CPLEE's retrieved documentation describes a box on four legs and gives only a stowed volume of 2540 cubic centimetres [1]. The LND's sensor head and electronics box are separate units whose external dimensions are not stated in the retrieved text. The reported lander top window of 16 cm by 23 cm is an opening in the lander payload compartment, not an instrument dimension [4]. The two instruments are not directly comparable because one is an analyser on legs and the other is a solid-state telescope with a separate electronics box.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The CPLEE mass is 2.7 kg, which the 1971 preliminary report also gives as approximately 2.7 kg (6 lb) [1][2]. The LND instrument mass is not stated in the retrieved text [4]. The paper's dose calculation uses the mass of one silicon detector, 1.04 g; this is a component value and not the instrument mass [4]. Mass determines launch-mass and lander-capacity requirements, so no comparison of total mission mass is made here.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The CPLEE used 3.0 W in normal operation and 6.0 W at night with the survival heater on [1]. The LND receives power, heater supply, thermistor and detector bias voltage from the lander through harnesses that connect the sensor head and electronics box [4]. The LND power consumption is not stated in the retrieved text.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Surface charged particle detectors must survive large temperature swings, draw power from a lander or ALSEP, and keep their calibration. The CPLEE documentation reports that high temperatures in 1972 caused a low-voltage condition in its power supply, so operation was continuous at night and intermittent by day [1]. Its survival heater was an explicit power requirement at night [1].

The LND sensor head is protected by a closable top window. The paper states that keeping the sensor head cool reduces the importance of leakage current as a noise source [4]. The window closes during the cold lunar night to keep heat inside the payload compartment [4]. For the sensor-head bracket interface, the LND paper models −20 °C to +55 °C in operation and −60 °C to +70 °C when not operating. For the electronics box and lander interface it expects −20 °C to +55 °C in operation and −70 °C to +70 °C when not operating [4]. During the first lunar day, the measured temperatures ranged from −7.97 °C to 48.10 °C, with the highest temperatures on the sensor head analogue board and the lowest in the electronics box [4].

Calibration and background are also operational constraints. The CPLEE carried a nickel-63 source for on-Moon calibration [1]. The LND paper states that the lander's radioisotope thermoelectric generator and three radioisotope heater units produce a background that dominates small energy deposits in single detectors. This background must be accounted for when interpreting the data [4].
article.limitations: A charged particle detector measures only the particles that reach its aperture within its energy range. Its data therefore depend on field of view, shielding, calibration and operating mode. Two examples cannot represent all designs. The CPLEE's energy range differs between its archive and preliminary documents, as explained under Limitations, Uncertainties and Evidence Gaps. The CPLEE's analyser power-supply failures in 1971 reduced the usable data from that point on [1]. The LND paper's dose and background results depend on lander-specific radioisotope background, which must be corrected for before any dose prediction [4].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Both surface examples were delivered as parts of larger mission packages rather than as standalone payloads. The CPLEE was part of the Apollo 14 ALSEP, and the LND was integrated into the Chang'e-4 lander's payload compartment [1][4]. The overview below describes the general chain of integration, transfer and setup.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into a surface experiment package or lander payload compartment on Earth. The CPLEE was an ALSEP experiment [1]; the LND was mounted inside the Chang'e-4 lander's −Y payload compartment [4].
Launch on the mission's launch vehicle. The Chang'e-4 lander launched on 7 December 2018 at 18:23 UTC [4].
Transfer to the Moon and land. The Chang'e-4 lander landed on 3 January 2019 at 02:26 UTC [4].
Deploy or confirm the instrument on the surface. The CPLEE was deployed on 5 February 1971 [1]. The LND sensor head remained fixed to the lander bracket [4].

Level, align and connect power and data. The CPLEE was levelled and aligned with a bubble level and a sun compass [1]. The LND connects to the lander's Instrument Control Unit for electrical and data interfaces [4].
Protect the instrument thermally. The CPLEE dust cover was removed after lunar module ascent [1]. The LND window is opened during the lunar day and closed during the lunar night [4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The CPLEE was deployed on the lunar surface as part of the Apollo 14 ALSEP, about 3 m northeast of the central station. It was levelled and aligned with a bubble level and sun compass [1]. The LND was not separately deployed. Its sensor head is fixed on a bracket close to the lander's upper deck, behind a re-closeable window [4].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The CPLEE (Apollo 14, 1971) and the LND (Chang'e-4, 2019) are the two lunar-surface examples discussed in this article. The CRaTER on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter is an orbital example. Its spacecraft integration and deployment are not verified in this article, so it is not described further [4][5][6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: This article does not assess compatibility with any named future lander, rover or spacecraft. A new charged particle detector would need verified interface data before compatibility could be judged. Relevant data include mass and power (for example, the CPLEE's 2.7 kg and 3.0 W and 6.0 W operating values [1]), mounting geometry and field of view (for example, the LND's 13 degree tilt and top window [4]), and thermal limits (for example, the LND's modelled −20 °C to +55 °C operating range [4]).

article.historical_significance:
The Apollo 14 CPLEE was a surface charged particle detector in the Apollo lunar surface programme. Its preliminary observations included a stable, low-energy photoelectron flux at the lunar surface and plasma clouds produced by the impact of the lunar module ascent stage [2]. Its data record of 1971 to 1977 is documented in the archive, although operation was degraded for much of the mission [1].

The Chang'e-4 LND is historically significant because its own paper describes its goal as the first active dosimetric measurements on the lunar surface [4]. Its results on the far side of the Moon complement the earlier Apollo surface data and the orbital dose measurements from Chandrayaan-1 and LRO described in its paper [4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
**Energy range conflict for the CPLEE.** The NSSDCA archive document states a measurement range of 40 eV to 20 keV [1]. The 1971 Apollo 14 preliminary report states energies from 50 to 50 000 eV [2]. The retrieved texts do not explain the difference. This article uses the archive range and reports the preliminary value separately, rather than combining them.

**Secondary sources.** A Wikipedia summary of the CPLEE [7] gives additional figures, including an energy-window count of 18. The analyser layout in [1] supports the aperture arrangement. The 18-window count is not confirmed by the retrieved primary text and is not used in this article.

**LND specifications.** The LND mass, power and external dimensions are not stated in the paper text retrieved for this article [4]. The LND's dose results, detector calibration and background corrections were not extracted in detail. This article describes LND instrument capabilities and early operating conditions only. The paper was read as an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2001.11028). The published Space Science Reviews version (DOI 10.1007/s11214-020-00725-3, listed on the arXiv record) was not checked.

**CRaTER.** The CRaTER instrument paper (Spence et al., Space Science Reviews 150, 243–284, 2010) [5] was identified from repository metadata and the LND paper's reference list, but its full text was not read in this session. CRaTER statements in this article rely on the LND paper's account [4] and on a secondary Wikipedia summary [6]. No CRaTER specifications are given.

**Images.** No article images are included. Candidate NASA and museum images were not verified as direct asset URLs in this session, so none are placed in the article. Adding images would require direct asset-URL verification.

**Source access.** The Apollo 14 documents were available as text-layer PDF copies. The LND paper was read through its arXiv PDF, whose text was extracted locally and searched for hardware values; word spacing was lost in that extraction, so quoted values were checked against their surrounding text. Web search was limited in this session, so sources were collected by fetching known authoritative pages directly, not by a systematic literature search. Apollo 12 SIDE and Chandrayaan-1 CHACE primary documents were not reached and are not described. Chandrayaan-1 RADOM is described only through the LND paper's account [4].

data_quality_notes: Rerun v2: LND hardware details (ten 500 micrometre silicon detectors, thermal-neutron gadolinium foils, 13 degree tilt, 16 cm by 23 cm top window, interface temperature model, RADOM dose figures) were checked against the arXiv PDF text. The text was extracted locally with a simple stream parser, which removed word spacing, so values were confirmed by their surrounding context rather than by a layout-preserving reader.

LND instrument mass, power and sensor-head and electronics-box external dimensions were searched for in the extracted arXiv text and not found. They remain null. The 1.04 g value is one silicon detector mass used in the dose calculation, not an instrument mass.
